transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Lyra CTO), Sofia Martinez (ML Eng), Ravi Iyer (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
Redwood and Lyra agreed to a pilot to validate reserved GPU sizing with burst capacity and fallback to smaller model variants; primary metrics are p95 latency and unit cost. Action items captured.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: okay, uh thanks everyone for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, i'll hand it off to Arjun to do a quick run of what we'll test and then we'll get into your workload details, sound good?
[00:12] Daniel: yep sounds good, thanks Maya. quick note we have limited time but, um, excited to nail down the success criteria.
[00:20] Arjun: great, hi all, i'm Arjun on the SE side. high level: we're proposing a 6-week pilot. week one is data/trace handoff, week two to three prep and small-scale benchmarks, week four dedicated reserved GPU lab with burst window testing, week five validation and fallbacks, week six final run and cost report. that's the playbook.
[00:42] Sofia: can you clarify "reserved GPU lab" — is that reserved with Redwood Dedicated or are we, like, setting up our own nodes?
[00:50] Maya: good Q. For this pilot we'll provision Redwood Dedicated GPUs (reserved) in our sandbox project. you keep data in your VPC or we can do private deployment if needed but initially dedicated pool inside Redwood is faster. if you want VPC peering we can do that for the lab step.
[01:05] Ravi: security is important — we need SOC2 doc and KMS integration details. will that be ready during pilot?
[01:12] Arjun: yes, we have an SOC2 summary and KMS flow. we'll share the security snapshot. for the pilot the data paths will use your KMS for key wrapping if you want — that adds a little set up time but doable in week one to two.
[01:26] Daniel: sounds fine. let's talk success criteria — our product team wants <350ms p95 for 512-token generation at baseline load of 40 qps with peaks up to 250 qps. cost target is also important: under $0.01 per generated token avg (rough target). how feasible is that?
[01:49] Arjun: okay — a couple of knobs. reserved GPU count, batching, and quantization variant. to hit 40 qps sustained with p95 <350ms we'll likely need N reserved A100-class equivalents or quantized 8-bit T4-like blobs — uh, sorry, mixing. essentially we can push a quantized llm to hit cost targets with slightly higher tail unless we use reserved higher-throughput cards.
[02:14] Sofia: what about fallback policies? if reserved pool saturates, we need failover to either a smaller model or to best-effort hosted pool. we cannot error out to customers.
[02:24] Arjun: yes. typical strategy: primary reserved pool serves low-latency requests, burst-to-shared (hosted) capacity for spikes, and a graceful fallback to a compact model variant if hosted is saturated too. you can set SLO thresholds like 95th latency at 350ms and a hard cap where traffic routes to compact.
[02:39] Maya: and we can set per-route cost/latency policies. also prefix caching for repeated prompts — if you have lots of similar prompts, that can save tokens and latency.
[02:49] Daniel: okay, good. can we run a benchmark that simulates our qps distribution? our traffic is spiky — 70% baseline at 40 qps, daily peak 250 qps for 3-6 minute bursts.
[03:04] Arjun: yes we'll need traces. Sofia, can you share tail lat distributions and a 7-day qps trace?
[03:10] Sofia: yes i can. i'll anonymize user IDs but keep lat and size. we'll include prompt lengths and distribution.
[03:16] Ravi: also can you recommend network egress sizing so we don't saturate the VPC? our infra team needs numbers.
[03:22] Arjun: for 250 qps at 512 avg tokens, rough egress bandwidth is X — i'll compute exact numbers in the config doc.
[03:29] Speaker 4: sorry to interject, do we have a timeline constraint from the product release?
[03:33] Daniel: yes, target release early feb, so pilot must finish by end of january to inform capacity planning. so compressed but doable.
[03:40] Maya: that fits the 6-week plan if we start this week.
[03:44] Arjun: now on benchmarks — we'll run three profiles: 1) latency-first with reserved-only, 2) cost-first with quantized configs, and 3) resilience with burst windows and induced saturation. each profile has a standard set of prompts and a randomized user mix.
[03:58] Sofia: for quantization, what models do you recommend? we tested 13B-flavor models in house but open to larger trimmed variants.
[04:06] Arjun: for production semantics we recommend a 33B quantized (q4f) or a trimmed 13B with higher throughput depending on quality. part of pilot is to sanity-check hallucination/quality delta on your prompt set.
[04:18] Daniel: okay we definitely need quality gates — if quantized model increases hallucinations we can't accept it. success criteria: quality regression under 3% vs current baseline measured by our eval set.
[04:29] Maya: we'll include quality evals in the benchmark template. please add any specific failure modes you want flagged.
[04:34] Sofia: yes — hallucination rate, token-level perplexity and a small sample of human evals on the 50 top prompts.
[04:42] Arjun: noted. on autoscaling: Redwood Dedicated supports reserved pools with configur-able burst capacity. we can set a burst budget (e.g., 30 minutes/day of full capacity) and then fallback rules. The tricky bit is warm-starting KV cache across nodes; cold starts will add tail.
[04:59] Ravi: warm cache — can you snapshot caches or do we need a pre-warm phase?
[05:04] Arjun: we do automatic prefix caching; for KV we can pre-warm commonly used contexts during pre-warm window before peak. part of lab run we'll measure cold vs warm p95 and feed that into fallback thresholds.
[05:16] Daniel: what's the expected degradation if we fallback to compact model?
[05:20] Arjun: typically latency improves but quality drops slightly; depending on model pair you might see a 5-12% regression on our automatic metrics — again we'll measure on your eval set.
[05:30] Maya: on cost modeling — we'll produce a per-token cost estimate for each profile and a blended estimate using your qps trace.
[05:36] Sofia: ok. about quotas and throttling — can we have a soft throttle where requests are queued for up to 2s before failing?
[05:43] Arjun: yes we support queueing and adaptive queuing parameters. but user experience tradeoffs — if you have synchronous flows, 2s is a lot. recommend using graceful degrade to compact model for interactive flows and queueing for batch.
[05:58] Speaker 4: question on monitoring — what telemetry will be available during pilot?
[06:02] Maya: console provides per-route latency, token costs, error rates, and trace-level logs. we can provide S3 access to raw traces for the pilot too.
[06:12] Daniel: perfect. can you run a small initial benchmark — like a 2-hour soak — before the big reserved lab?
[06:18] Arjun: yes we'll run a short smoke with your traces in week two. that will help tune batch sizes and queue params.
[06:24] Sofia: what's the acceptance criteria for the reserved sizing? if we ask for N GPUs and you provision, what do we measure?
[06:31] Arjun: measurement checklist: sustained baseline p95 at or under your target (350ms), peak stress test p95 during bursts (we accept some increased latency up to 500ms before fallback), error rate <2% (API errors), and within cost envelope +/-15%. if it doesn't meet those we'll iterate on reserved counts and batching.
[06:51] Maya: also, we'll propose an initial reserved count with headroom for 20% traffic growth. that's conservative.
[06:58] Daniel: ok let's talk numbers — Arjun, can you give an example config for our baseline numbers?
[07:04] Arjun: quick ballpark: to hit 40 qps p95 <350ms on a 33B quantized model you might need 4 x high-memory A100-equivalent cards (or 6 x T4-class quantized nodes) depending on batch sizes. for 250 qps bursts you'd rely on burst pool or additional ephemeral nodes — we can define burst budget in minutes per day.
[07:26] Ravi: that's helpful — we need the exact mapping of GPU types to qps and per-hour cost for triage.
[07:31] Arjun: we'll include a matrix: GPU type / model variant / sustained qps / p95 / cost per hour.
[07:37] Sofia: do you support model hot-swapping during run? like route some percent to compact model for 10 minutes then back?
[07:42] Maya: yes rollouts can be scheduled and traffic split with canary policies. we also have automatic fallback routing if a route hits latency or error thresholds.
[07:52] Daniel: any constraints on model quantization we should be aware of? some of our prompts rely on numeric precision and quantization hurts that bit.
[07:58] Arjun: we'll test for those regression cases. for numeric-critical prompts we might pin to full-fidelity model on reserved pool and route less critical traffic to quantized model.
[08:07] Sofia: good idea.
[08:10] Arjun: let's capture deliverables: benchmark template, reserved sizing recommendation, burst/fallback policy draft, security snapshot, and lab schedule.
[08:20] Maya: and we'll add a quick decision doc for which prompts are pinned to high-fidelity paths.
[08:26] Daniel: timeline recap — if we start today, Lyra provides traces by Dec 3, Redwood shares benchmark plan Dec 1, first smoke Dec 7, reserved lab Dec 14-18 (flex), final run Jan 8-12, and report Jan 16. that ok?
[08:42] Maya: yes thats doable. note lab dates flexible but we'll need calendar holds.
[08:46] Ravi: security note — we'll need a non-production KMS key created by our security team; we will share contact details off-line.
[08:53] Maya: okay we'll follow up.
[08:55] Speaker 4: one last quick thing — what if the cost target cannot be met even with quantization?
[08:59] Arjun: then options: increase reserved pool efficiency (better batching), accept a higher cost, or change SLA like increase allowed p95. we will make tradeoffs explicit in the cost model.
[09:12] Daniel: alright. any blockers from Redwood side?
[09:15] Maya: none. we'll start internal provisioning after Sofia uploads the traces and Ravi confirms VPC window.
[09:22] Arjun: i'll begin drafting the GPU mapping matrix and the fallback policy doc.
[09:27] Maya: thanks all. we'll recap with an email and calendar invites for the lab window.
[09:32] Daniel: thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[09:35] Sofia: thanks everyone.
[09:36] Ravi: thanks.
[09:38] Maya: cool, end of call.
